place.en: The hidden realm · Below the drop

setup.zh: 别人都往右，你往左，往下。崖底是一面光秃秃的石墙——墙后头，有风。墙脚下一汪滴水积成的浅潭，潭里趴着一只白身赤首、像龟的东西：蛫。它把那面墙护得严严实实。
setup.en: Everyone goes right; you go left, and down. At the foot of the cliff, a bare stone wall — and behind it, wind. At the wall's foot, a shallow pool of gathered drips, and in it a white-bodied, red-headed thing like a turtle: a gui. It guards the wall close.

recap.zh: 秘境里，银月领着你往左、往下。墙前守着一只蛫；你没打它，没撬它，把三天的水倒给了它。它喝够了，爬回墙脚趴了不知多少年的那个窝——它就是门闩。墙，开了。
recap.en: In the hidden realm Yinyue led you left and down. A gui guarded the wall; you didn't strike it or pry it — you poured it your three days' water. When it had drunk its fill it crawled back into the hollow at the wall's foot where it had lain for who knows how many years — it was the latch. The wall opened.

zh: 往左。往下。潭里，一只白身赤首的蛫。
en: Left. Down. In the pool, a white-bodied, red-headed gui.

label.en: The cold stone at the wall's foot

text.zh: 巴掌大一块石头，比旁边的都凉，凉得发麻，四边一道极细的缝，按下去纹丝不动。跟前的地上，磨出一个椭圆的浅窝，溜光溜光。
text.en: A stone the size of a palm, colder than those around it, cold enough to numb, a hairline seam round it; pressed, it doesn't stir. On the ground before it, a shallow oval hollow worn smooth as glass.

label.en: The water marks round the pool

text.zh: 潭边的石头上，一圈一圈，全是水印子：齐膝，齐小腿，齐脚踝。最底下那汪水，如今只剩一巴掌深。
text.en: The rock round the pool is ringed with water marks: knee-high, shin-high, ankle-high. What is left at the bottom is a hand's depth.

text.zh: 你拔一根头发举到墙前。它往墙的方向飘了一飘，又一飘——倒像墙那边有一张嘴，隔着一层石头，在慢慢地吸气。
text.en: You pull out a hair and hold it to the wall. It drifts toward the wall, once, and again — as if behind it a mouth were slowly breathing in, through a layer of stone.

story.zh:
小狰是不能带进秘境的——秘境的门认名牌，名册上没有畜生。小满只得把它寄在执事房。它死死扒着他的袖子不撒手，五条尾巴一齐竖着；周衡从抽屉里摸出一根萝卜，放在桌角上，道：「它吃一根，我记一根。」小狰盯着萝卜，那眼神分明是说「你拿一根萝卜就把我卖了」，然后松开袖子，跳上桌角，抱着萝卜「咔嚓咔嚓」地啃，啃一口，回过头拿湿汪汪的眼睛瞅他一眼，再啃一口，又瞅一眼，啃完了，打了个嗝。

名牌是祖师传下来的，一块进一个人。外门三百多人用不完，剩下的一百来块，周衡的账簿上另有一页：卖给下邳的青萍剑派、彭城的赤松观和城里几户人家的子弟，一块二十块灵石，入公中。周衡见他看，把账簿一拢：「观里穷。卖的是一块牌子；进去捡着什么，各凭本事。」

山门前那三百级石阶上，瞿老照旧在扫他的台阶。三百多人从他身边涌下去，他头也不抬，只把扫帚往旁边让一让。小满走到他跟前，放慢了脚。瞿老忽然开口了，声音不高，像对着台阶说的：「水，退得比上回低。」小满一怔。瞿老还在扫，又道：「上回比上上回低。」小满道：「……那是好，还是不好？」瞿老没有答，把扫帚一让，让出一条路来：「腿稳。」

辰时，外门三百多个弟子挤在河滩上。泥是黑的，泥上结着一层白霜，霜上歪歪扭扭躺着几条来不及跟着水走的鱼，嘴一张一合。观里的杂役连夜往泥上铺了木板，从岸边一直铺到石门跟前，窄窄一条道。那道石门露在泥滩上，门缝里往外冒着一丝一丝的白气，冬天的早晨，那白气是暖的。

灰袍中间，还夹着百来个别样颜色的。青袍长剑、一开口是下邳腔的，是青萍剑派；赭黄袍子、腰里挂着葫芦的，是赤松观；还有七八个锦袍公子，一人一块名牌，家丁进不去，只好在岸上替主子提着食盒。唱名的执事——马小宝的表伯——捧着一本薄名册站在道口，念一个外人的名字，递一块名牌。念到一个胖胖的锦袍公子，他身后那个黄袍笑着让了半步，让他先领。那黄袍二十五六，白净脸，腰里的葫芦跟同门的不一样：赤铜的，拳头大，葫芦嘴拿一个铜塞子塞着，他脚边的白霜，围着那只葫芦化开了一圈；托着葫芦的那只右手，掌心焦黑一块，像给火烙过；左臂上挎着一面盘子大的赤铜小盾，刻着火纹，纹路里像有一点红，慢慢地走。同门里有人跟旁人夸：「我们邹师兄，练气九层；那面盾，祖师所赠，结丹以下，无人能破。」他不看沉鼎观的人，只看那胖公子腰里鼓鼓的荷包。脚边一条鱼还在张嘴，他拿鞋跟踩住它的头，碾了一碾，脸上照旧冲着执事笑。执事念道：「彭城赤松观，邹青松。」他上前接了牌子。

石门前头站着一个人，一身灰袍，面目温和，两只手拢在袖子里，正是观主玄沉子。他从山上下来的时候，一个筑基的师叔踩着剑先到，河滩上的人便自己往两边让出一条道来；他走过去，泥滩上几百号人，连咳嗽都咽了回去，河心那一道亮线，在他身后静得像一根拉直的弦。老弟子们说，每回开门，观主都这般站着，从头一个进，站到最后一个出；问他站着做什么，他说数人——可他从来不拿本子。

孙二狗挤到小满身边，鼻涕冻成了两道冰溜子，小声道：「沈师兄，我跟着你，行么？我灵根差，一个人进去，怕……」他自己先红了脸，「……怕回不来。」孙二狗腰上系着一个蓝布包，露出一截红绳——他娘缝的护身符。小满背上背着爷爷那张弓——猎户进一座没进过的山，弓不离身；箭壶里三支竹箭，是他在柴房里自己削的，箭头是伙房讨来的旧铁钉。他从包袱里摸出一根萝卜，塞进孙二狗手里：「跟着人多的走，走中间。刀先落在两头。」孙二狗捧着萝卜，道：「……那师兄你呢？」小满道：「我走没人的地方。没人，就没刀。」孙二狗没听懂，可他很郑重地点了点头，把萝卜揣进怀里，跟那个护身符揣在一处。

执事敲了三下锣。玄沉子从袖子里摸出一块名牌，比众人的大一圈，铜色也旧，按进石门正中一个凹槽里。马小宝领着他那几个人，抢着往门口挤，挤过小满身边的时候，最末一个落后了半步。是老蔫。他一只手提着马小宝的描金食盒，肩上斜挎着一大盘麻绳，眼睛不看小满，只看着自己的脚尖，嘴唇几乎没动：「……宝哥叫人盯着你。绳子，是带给你的。」说完，快走两步，跟上去了。

石门「嘎嘎」地响着，开了一道缝，缝里绷着一层亮汪汪的东西，像一张拉紧了的水皮子，皮子上流着一层淡淡的光，凉气隔着三步扑在脸上，近前的人脸都映青了。头一拨是内门的练气弟子，二十几个，不排队，从木板道上一个跟一个走过去，手里卷着内门自己的图；空场上那几张桌子，他们一眼也没看过。走在最前头的五个，是九层。一个锦袍公子想跟着他们的尾巴挤进去，头里那个九层没回头，袖子往后一拂，那人便飞出去两三丈，栽进黑泥里，泥没到胸口。岸上的家丁拿竹竿把他拽了上来，没人多看一眼。内门的人一个接一个，没进了那层水皮子里。四百来人这才一窝蜂地往里挤，水皮子一晃一晃，人一个个没了。小满没有挤。九层的，他想，往后见一回，躲一回。人群里却也有一个人没挤——卖地图的那两个里头，踹他左边肋骨的那一个，抄着手站在人堆边上，眼睛不看石门，看他。他站在一块石头上等着。等最后一个人挤进了门，才跳下来，慢吞吞地走了进去。走到门里，他回头望了一眼：那个抄着手的人，也不紧不慢地跟了进来。

走进石门的那一刻，他胸口的木牌「腾」地一烫。那一烫跟往常不同：烫了一下，没有停，第二下，第三下，一下紧似一下，倒像是一颗心在他胸口底下跳。银月钻了出来，蹲在他肩膀上，身子比从前实了些。她没有打哈欠，一双金色的眼睛睁得大大的，看石壁，看石壁上的花纹，鼻子一抽一抽的，像在闻着什么很远、很远的东西。

她开口了，声音却变了，倒像一个人站在自己小时候住过的院子里：「……这地方。本王来过。」小满问：「什么时候？」银月道：「不知道。」小满问：「来做什么？」银月道：「不知道。」小满道：「那你知道什么？」银月的鼻子又抽了两抽，才道：「……底下。」

门里是一座石厅，四壁开着七八个口子。人手一张图，图上画的路各不相同：照图走的，跟着同门走的，闭着眼睛猜的，一窝一窝散进了各个口子。内门那二十几个照着自己的图，头也不回地进了一个；那条画得最密的长廊，挤进去的人最多。一个口子一个口子地，石厅里的人稀了下去。剩下一个口子没人进：一道窄窄的石缝，缝口给一块塌下来的大石头堵了一半，石头上刻着一个歪歪扭扭的「凶」字，字底下画了个骷髅头。

阿禾跟着人多的走。进门以前，她看见了两样东西：卖地图那两个里头抄着手的那一个，人人往门里挤，他不挤，眼睛钉在沈小满身上；老蔫肩上，斜挎着一大盘麻绳。进秘境捡灵草，用不着那么长的绳子。

她照着肚子里那张图走。第二间石室门口，地上第三块石板踩上去会翻——她站在旁边，喊了一声「别踩第三块」。一个听了；一个没来得及听，给后头一个锦袍公子一肘子拐开，掉了下去，坑里「哎哟」一声，是孙二狗的嗓子。她给人群推着往前走，回头喊了第二声，没有人应。

石桥窄，只容一个人。桥当中两个人黑地里撞上，谁也不让，青袍的剑先出了鞘；倒下的那个手里攥着的，是一只火折子。阿禾在桥头蹲了一炷香，才敢过去。

桥那头的灵草园子，最后一株给人连根拔了。两个本观的老弟子把一个锦袍公子按进泥里，按到他不动了，才松手，蹲在泥里分那株草，一人一半；又翻他的荷包，灵石五块，一人两块，多出来那一块，两个人猜拳。园子底下那道暗河，在山腹里穿过去，地图上画的是水；今年泗水退得低，暗河干了，露了底，石缝里一丛一丛全是灵草，上中下三品都有，壁上一道铜矿。人都往下涌。往下只有一道石坎，一人宽。坎口站着内门的祁长松，八层，袍子下摆一层土黄的灰，两只脚钉在那里；人涌到他跟前，推他，挤他，像水撞上一根桩，撞不动，只好从两边分开，又流回来。坎底下，那四个九层一丛一丛地拔，拔一丛，往袖里一揣，看都不看是几品。拔够了上来，祁长松才挪开一步。

阿禾没有去抢。她四层，功法是养草木的，打架是她最不会的一样；坎底下那四个九层，坎口那一个八层，哪一个都是一袖子拂她两三丈的人。她绕着暗河边上，往没人的那一头走，走到尽头，有一片地，是黑的，黑得发亮，一根草也不长，跟石坳村她家那面坡田，一个样子。黑地的边上，偏偏冒着一株草，三片叶子，紫里透金，叶背上一层细绒，在黑地里自己透着一点暗金的光，像三盏熬到了底的小油灯：「紫须芝，一株抵三块灵石。」三块灵石，是外门一个月的份例。她蹲下去，指头底下的黑土一松，露出半粒东西来，黑的，硬得像石子：是谷，烧焦了一样的谷。她拿指甲再往下抠——那片黑地底下，一垄一垄，排得整整齐齐。很久以前，这里有人种过地。那株紫须芝的根，正缠在那一垄谷里：拔草，便连根带谷翻成一团烂泥。她没有拔。她从那一垄的这一头，离草根远远的，一粒一粒，抠出三粒来，草根一根也没伤着。

石厅里往凶崖去的也有。一个本观的老弟子走到缝口，探头往下看了一眼，缩回头骂了一句，追人堆去了；一个青萍的青袍站了一会儿，也走了。小满不比他们胆大，也不比他们聪明。九层进的口子，他不进；马小宝进的口子，他也不进；剩下这一个，没人要。何况是崖——崖，他是爬惯了的。

小满还没走到缝口，石厅拐角那头先有人说话，声音很和气：「……脚崴了？我扶你。」他一把将肩上的银月按进衣襟，贴着石壁站住了。拐角后头，那个胖胖的锦袍公子坐在地上抱着脚脖子，人都散进口子里去了，没有一个人等他。蹲在他跟前的，是那个掌心焦黑的黄袍。胖公子道：「多谢……多谢师兄。」邹青松道：「荷包里是什么？」胖公子一把捂住了腰：「我爹给的……保命的符……」邹青松笑了一笑，拔开了葫芦塞子。

一条火蛇从葫芦嘴里窜了出来，一尺来长，赤红赤红，在胖公子脖子上绕了一圈。胖公子只叫了半声。那股焦糊味儿飘过来，一半是绸子，一半是肉。邹青松把火蛇收回葫芦，解下那只荷包倒出来看：一道保命符，裂成了两半；灵石七块。他把灵石揣进怀里，拿胖公子的锦袍擦了擦葫芦嘴，又扯下他腰上的名牌，看也没看，往黑处一扔。然后他站起身来，哼着一支小曲儿，进了人多的那个口子。

小满贴着石壁，一直等到那小曲儿听不见了，才挪动脚。他从那胖公子身边过去，那人的眼睛还睁着，望着石厅顶上。他侧着身子，挤进了那道石缝。

石缝后头是一段往下走的石阶，窄，陡，湿，长满了青苔。走了约莫一顿饭的工夫，前面是一道断崖，崖下黑洞洞的，只听得见底下有水滴的声音，一滴，隔很久，又一滴。银月从他衣襟里钻出来，道：「往下。这里的灵气是从下面上来的……很厚。外头的，薄得像一碗刷锅水；这里的，像一口封了几百年的井，刚揭开盖子。」

他把袖子挽起来，顺着崖壁往下爬。他是猎户家的孩子，爬崖是本行，可这道崖从上到下一根草也不长，石头凉得透骨。他左边的肋骨，十月十二那夜断的，到这时候还没长牢，一使劲，便像有人往里头塞了一根针。

爬到一半，底下有了火光。他把身子往崖上一道石缝里一塞，贴平了。底下是一道窄窄的石台，站着两个内门的，一个举着火折子；另一个提着剑，便是河滩上拂袖子的那个九层。九层绕着台上一面光秃秃的石墙敲了一圈，敲到墙脚，一剑劈了下去。

墙脚有一汪半干的水潭，潭边卧着一块碾盘大的黑石头——小满方才也只当它是一块石头。剑声一响，那「石头」前头探出一颗脑袋来，斗大，赤红赤红，像一颗烧透了的炭。九层回手一剑斩在它壳上，火星一迸，剑从壳上滑开，在壳沿靠脖子的地方崩出一道裂纹。它没有缩。那颗脑袋一伸，比剑还快，「喀」的一声，咬住了九层的肩膀和半边脖子，往潭里一拖。剑脱了手，当啷一声落在塌石边上。举火折子的那个，火折子一扔，扭头钻进塌石后头一道缝里——他们两个，原是从那里来的——一眼也没往回看。潭里扑腾了几下，便不扑腾了。

他没有下去。他贴在石缝里，把底下看了个遍。那道石台贴着崖根，只有三四步宽；往外再迈一步，又是黑的——那才是凶崖，深不见底，方才那一滴一滴的水声，便是从这底下上来的。石台外沿钉着一根锈烂了的铁橛子，橛子上拴着半截麻绳，垂在黑里。石台那一头，崖根底下堆着半人高一堆塌石；这一头便是那面石墙，一丈来高，不见门，不见缝；墙脚的地上，凿着一个极大的浅窝，凿得溜光，窝底积着一层干泥，正上方的崖壁上，凸出一块石檐。银月道：「那面墙后头，有风。」

那黑石头一动不动，壳像一口倒扣的大铁锅，铁黑铁黑；壳沿上一道一道的旧印子，刀砍的，铁器撬的，旧得发黑。潭底除了方才那个九层，还躺着两副白骨，一副手里还攥着一把锈刀。

银月看了半天，道：「白身，赤首，像龟。……本王年轻的时候，在一座山上见过它们一窝，巴掌大，山里的人捡它们的壳挂在房梁底下，说是能挡火。巴掌大的长成这样，怕是比本王还老。……[蛫]{注=gui}。有本书叫《山海经》{典=shanhai-gui}，写它『其狀如龜，而白身赤首』，『是可以禦火』。」

崖上滚下来一粒小石子，落在它壳上，它不动。一只土鳖从塌石里爬出来，从它鼻子底下爬过去，它也不动；土鳖爬到潭边一沾水，那颗脑袋「喀」地出来了。隔一阵，它自己也往潭里探一探，探到底，又缩回去——那汪水只剩一巴掌深，潭边的石头上一圈一圈全是水印子，最高的一圈齐它的壳顶。它渴得快死了。壳沿那道新裂纹，往外渗着黑水。小满又看那个浅窝：椭圆的，一头尖，四边各一个小凹，跟那口铁锅一般大小。他想：这面墙，要的是它那一身分量。

他打不过它。河滩上那一拂袖子，他是看见了的；拂袖子的那一个，在它嘴底下，只够一口。他爹说过：「打不过的，不打。给它下坠子。」
story.en:
No spirit beast may go into the hidden realm — its door knows name tablets, and there are no beasts on the roll. Xiaoman had to leave the little zheng at the stewards' office. It clung to his sleeve, all five tails up; Zhou Heng took a radish from his drawer and set it on the corner of the table: "It eats one, I write down one." The zheng stared at the radish with a look that plainly said you'd sell me for one radish — then let go of the sleeve, hopped onto the table, hugged the radish and went crunch, crunch — one bite, then a look back at him with wet, swimming eyes; another bite, another look; and when it was done, it burped.

The tablets had come down from the founder: one tablet, one person in. The outer court's three hundred-odd couldn't use them all, and the hundred-odd left over had a page of their own in Zhou Heng's ledger: sold to the Green Duckweed Sword School of Xiapi, the Red Pine Abbey of Pengcheng, and the sons of a few well-off families in town — twenty spirit stones a tablet, into the common fund. Seeing him look, Zhou Heng drew the ledger shut: "The abbey is poor. What we sell is a tablet; whatever you pick up inside is your own luck."

On the three hundred steps before the gate Elder Qu was sweeping his stair as always. Three hundred-odd people poured down past him; he didn't look up, only moved his broom aside. Coming level with him, Xiaoman slowed. The old man spoke, not loudly, as if to the step: "The water's gone lower than last time." Xiaoman started. Still sweeping, Qu said: "Last time was lower than the time before." "…Is that good or bad?" No answer; the broom moved aside to make a way. "Steady legs."

At the hour of the dragon the three hundred-odd outer disciples crowded onto the flats. The mud was black and crusted with white frost, and on the frost lay a few fish that hadn't followed the water, mouths opening and closing. Overnight the abbey's handymen had laid planks on the mud, from the bank right up to the stone door: one narrow path. The stone door stood out of the mud, wisps of white breath rising from its seam — warm, on a winter morning.

Among the grey robes stood a hundred-odd of other colours. Green robes and long swords, Xiapi in every vowel: the Green Duckweed Sword School. Ochre robes with gourds at the belt: the Red Pine Abbey. And seven or eight young gentlemen in brocade, one name tablet each — their servants couldn't come in, so they stood on the bank holding their masters' food boxes. The name-calling steward — Ma Xiaobao's uncle — stood at the head of the path with a thin roll, reading out an outsider's name and handing over a tablet. When he called a plump young gentleman in brocade, the ochre robe behind him smiled and stepped half a pace aside to let him go first. That ochre robe was twenty-five or -six, fair-faced, and the gourd at his belt was not like his fellows': red bronze, the size of a fist, its mouth stopped with a bronze plug, and the white frost at his feet had melted in a ring round that gourd; the right hand that cupped it had a scorched-black patch on the palm, as if branded by fire; on his left arm hung a little red-bronze shield the size of a plate, cut with flame patterns, and in the lines a little red seemed to creep slowly along. One of his fellows was boasting to the people beside him: "Brother Zou is at layer nine of Qi Refining; and that shield of his, a gift from our founder — nothing short of Core Formation can break it." He didn't look at the Chending people; he looked only at the fat purse bulging at the plump gentleman's waist. A fish by his foot was still gaping; he set his heel on its head and ground it once, his face still smiling at the steward. The steward read: "Red Pine Abbey of Pengcheng, Zou Qingsong." He stepped up and took his tablet.

Before the door stood a man in a grey robe, mild of face, hands folded in his sleeves: Abbot Xuanchenzi. When he came down the mountain, an uncle-master of the Foundation had arrived ahead of him on a sword, and the crowd on the bank parted of itself to make a way; as he walked through, the hundreds on the mudflat swallowed even their coughs, and the bright line of the river's heart lay behind him still as a drawn string. The seniors said that whenever the realm opened he stood like this, from the first one in to the last one out; asked what he was doing, he said: counting people — but he never held a book.

Sun Ergou squeezed up beside Xiaoman, snot frozen into two shiny icicles, and said in a small voice: "Brother Shen, can I come with you? My roots are bad, going in alone I'm afraid…" He blushed before he said it: "…afraid I won't come back." At Sun Ergou's waist hung a blue cloth pouch with a bit of red string showing — the charm his mother sewed. On Xiaoman's back was his grandfather's bow — a hunter going into a mountain he has never entered keeps his bow by him; in the quiver were three bamboo arrows he had whittled himself in the woodshed, their heads old iron nails begged from the kitchen. He took a radish from his bundle and put it in Sun Ergou's hand: "Go with the crowd, and walk in the middle. The knife comes down on the edges first." Holding the radish, Sun Ergou said: "…And you, brother?" "I'll go where there's nobody. No people, no knives." Sun Ergou didn't follow, but he nodded gravely and tucked the radish into his coat beside the charm.

The steward struck the gong three times. Xuanchenzi took a tablet from his sleeve — a size larger than everyone else's, the bronze older — and pressed it into a hollow in the middle of the stone door. Ma Xiaobao led his few to the front of the crush, and as they shoved past Xiaoman the last of them fell half a step behind. It was Old Wilt. In one hand he carried Ma Xiaobao's gilt food box, and a big coil of hemp rope hung slantwise over his shoulder. He didn't look at Xiaoman, only at his own toes, and his lips barely moved: "…Brother Bao's had you watched. The rope — it's for you." Then he hurried two steps and caught up.

The door ground open a crack, and across the crack hung something bright and shimmering, like a skin of water stretched taut; a pale light flowed over it, its chill struck the face from three paces off, and the faces nearest it were lit blue. The first through were the inner court's Qi Refining disciples, twenty-odd of them, who did not queue: they walked the plank way one behind another, each with the inner court's own map rolled in hand; the tables on the square they had never so much as glanced at. The five at the front were layer nine. A young gentleman in brocade tried to slip in on their tail; the layer nine at the head didn't turn, only flicked his sleeve backward, and the man flew two or three zhang and went into the black mud up to his chest. A servant on the bank hauled him out with a bamboo pole, and nobody spared him a second look. One after another the inner court sank into the skin of water. Only then did four hundred-odd people shove in; the skin quivered and quivered, and one by one they were gone. Xiaoman didn't shove. Layer nines, he thought: see one, go the other way. Nor did one other man: of the two map sellers, the one who'd kicked his left ribs stood at the edge of the crowd with his arms folded, watching not the door but him. Xiaoman stood on a rock and waited. When the last one was through, he hopped down and strolled in. Inside, he glanced back: the man with folded arms was strolling in after him.

The moment he stepped through the stone door, the token on his chest flared hot. Not like before: it pulsed once and didn't stop — a second, a third, faster and faster, like a heart beating beneath his own. Yinyue slipped out and sat on his shoulder, more solid than before. She didn't yawn; her golden eyes were wide, looking at the walls, at the patterns on the walls, nose twitching as if at something far, far away.

When she spoke, her voice had changed, like someone standing in the yard she lived in as a child: "…This place. I have been here." "When?" "I don't know." "What for?" "I don't know." "Then what do you know?" Her nose twitched twice more before she said: "…Down."

Inside the door was a stone hall with seven or eight openings in its walls. Everyone had a map, and the maps drew different roads: some went by the map, some followed their own school, some shut their eyes and guessed, and they scattered into the openings clump by clump. The inner court's twenty-odd went into one by their own map without looking back; the corridor drawn densest on the maps took the biggest crowd. Opening by opening, the hall thinned out. One opening nobody took: a narrow crack in the rock, half blocked by a fallen boulder with a crooked word cut in it — DANGER — and under it a skull.

A He went with the crowd. Before they went in, she had seen two things: of the two map sellers, the one with his arms folded didn't push for the door with everyone else — his eyes were nailed on Shen Xiaoman; and slung across Old Wilt's shoulder was a big coil of hemp rope. You don't need that much rope to pick herbs.

She went by the map in her head. At the door of the second chamber, the third flagstone tips when you tread on it — she stood beside it and shouted, "Don't step on the third one!" One heard; one didn't hear in time, was elbowed aside by a young gentleman in brocade behind and dropped through, and an "ow!" came up out of the pit in Sun Ergou's voice. The crowd pushed her on; she looked back and shouted again; no one answered.

The stone bridge was narrow, room for one. In the middle of it two men ran into each other in the dark, and neither gave way; the green robe's sword was out first, and what the man who went down had been gripping was a fire-starter. A He crouched at the bridgehead for a stick of incense before she dared go over.

In the herb garden past the bridge, the last plant had been pulled up by the roots. Two old disciples of the abbey pressed a young gentleman in brocade into the mud and held him there till he stopped moving, then let go and crouched in the mud to share the plant, half each; then they turned out his purse — five spirit stones, two each, and for the odd one the two of them played finger-guessing. The underground river below the garden, running through the belly of the mountain, was drawn on the map as water; this year the Si had sunk low, the underground river had run dry and bared its bottom, and every crack was thick with spirit herbs, high, middle and low grade alike, and a vein of copper ran along the wall. Everyone poured down into it. There was only one way down, a stone step one person wide. At its lip stood the inner court's Qi Changsong, layer eight, the hem of his robe dusted earth-yellow, both feet nailed there; the crowd surged up to him, pushed him, shoved him, like water against a post — he didn't move, and it split around him and flowed back. Below the step the four layer nines were stripping the herbs clump by clump, each clump into a sleeve, not even looking at the grade. When they had enough and came up, Qi Changsong moved aside one step.

A He didn't join the scramble. She was layer four, and her art was for growing things; fighting was what she was worst at, and any of the four layer nines below, or the layer eight on the lip, could have swept her thirty feet with one sleeve. She went along the underground river's edge toward the end where nobody was, and at the very end lay a patch of ground, black, black and shiny, not a blade of grass on it — just like her family's hillside field in Shi'ao Village. At the edge of the black ground, of all places, a plant had come up, three leaves, purple shot with gold, a fine down on their undersides glowing dark gold in the black ground like three little lamps burned nearly dry: "Purple-whisker zhi, one plant worth three spirit stones." Three spirit stones were a month's allowance in the outer court. She crouched; the black earth loosened under her fingers and showed half of something, black, hard as a pebble: grain, grain that looked burnt. She dug further down with her fingernail — under that black ground, row on row, laid out neat and even. Long, long ago, someone had farmed here. The purple-whisker zhi's roots were wound right through that row of grain: pull the plant, and roots and grain came up together in a mess of mud. She didn't pull it. From the near end of the row, well away from its roots, one grain at a time, she dug out three, and didn't hurt a single root.

Some from the stone hall did go toward the Cliff of Danger. One of the abbey's seniors walked to the mouth of the crack, poked his head in to look down, pulled it back with a curse and went after the crowd; a green robe from Qingping stood there a while and left too. Xiaoman was no bolder than they were, and no cleverer. Where the layer nines went, he didn't go; where Ma Xiaobao went, he didn't go either; this one was left, and nobody wanted it. Besides, it was a cliff — and cliffs he'd been climbing all his life.

Before Xiaoman reached the crack, a voice spoke from round the bend of the stone hall, very kindly: "…Turned your ankle? Let me help you." He pushed Yinyue from his shoulder into the front of his coat and stood flat against the wall. Round the bend, the plump young gentleman in brocade sat on the ground clutching his ankle; everyone had scattered into the openings, and no one had waited for him. Crouched before him was the ochre robe with the scorched palm. "Thank you… thank you, brother," said the plump gentleman. "What's in the purse?" said Zou Qingsong. The plump gentleman clapped a hand over his waist: "My father gave it me… a life-saving charm…" Zou Qingsong smiled a little and pulled the plug from his gourd.

A fire snake shot out of the gourd's mouth, a foot or so long, red as red, and wound once round the plump gentleman's neck. He got out only half a cry. The burnt smell drifted over, half silk, half flesh. Zou Qingsong called the snake back into the gourd, untied the purse and tipped it out to look: one life-saving charm, cracked in two; seven spirit stones. He tucked the stones into his coat, wiped the gourd's mouth on the gentleman's brocade, then tore the name tablet from his waist and, without a glance, tossed it into the dark. Then he stood up and, humming a little tune, went into the opening with the most people.

Xiaoman stayed flat against the wall until he could no longer hear the tune, and only then moved. He passed the plump gentleman; the man's eyes were still open, gazing up at the ceiling of the stone hall. He turned sideways and squeezed into the crack.

Behind the crack a flight of steps went down, narrow, steep, wet, thick with moss. After about the time of a meal it ended at a drop; below was black, only the sound of water dripping, one drop, a long pause, another. Yinyue slipped out of his coat. "Down. The spirit-qi here comes up from below… thick. Outside, it's thin as dishwater; this is like a well sealed for hundreds of years, its lid just lifted."

He rolled up his sleeves and climbed down the cliff face. A hunter's son, climbing was his trade; but this cliff grew not one blade of grass top to bottom, and the stone was cold to the bone. His left rib, broken on the night of the twelfth of the tenth month, still hadn't knit, and every heave was like a needle pushed in.

Halfway down, there was firelight below. He wedged himself into a crack in the cliff and lay flat. Below was a narrow stone ledge with two inner-court disciples on it, one holding up a fire-stick; the other had a sword in his hand — the layer nine who had flicked his sleeve on the riverbank. The layer nine tapped his way round a bare stone wall on the ledge, and at the wall's foot brought his sword down.

At the foot of the wall lay a half-dry pool, and beside it a black rock the size of a millstone — Xiaoman too had taken it for a rock. At the ring of the sword a head pushed out from the front of that "rock", big as a grain measure, red as a coal burned through. The layer nine swung back and struck its shell; sparks flew, the blade skidded off, and where the rim met the neck a crack sprang open. It did not pull in. The head shot out, faster than the sword — snap — took the layer nine by the shoulder and half his neck, and dragged him into the pool. The sword flew from his hand and clanged down by the fallen rock. The one with the fire-stick flung it away and dived into a crack behind the fallen rock — that was the way the two of them had come — and never once looked back. In the pool there was some thrashing, and then there wasn't.

He didn't go down. Pressed in the crack, he looked the place over. The ledge hugged the foot of the cliff, three or four paces wide; one step further out and it was black again — that was the Cliff of Danger proper, bottomless, and the dripping he had heard came up from down there. On the ledge's outer edge an iron spike was driven in, rusted rotten, with half a length of hemp rope tied to it, hanging into the dark. At the far end of the ledge, at the foot of the cliff, lay a heap of fallen rock half a man high; at this end was the wall, ten feet high, no door, no crack; on the ground at its foot a huge shallow hollow had been cut, chiselled smooth as glass, a crust of dry mud in its bottom, and on the cliff right above it jutted a stone eave. "Behind that wall," said Yinyue, "there's wind."

The black rock lay motionless, its shell like a great iron pot turned upside down, iron-black; along the rim ran old marks, one after another — knife cuts, the scrape of iron levers — gone black with age. On the bottom of the pool, besides the layer nine, lay two skeletons, one still gripping a rusted blade.

Yinyue looked a long while. "White body, red head, like a turtle… When I was young I saw a nest of them on a mountain, palm-sized; the mountain folk picked up their shells and hung them under the roof beams, said they kept off fire. A palm-sized one grown to this — it may be older than I am. …A gui. There's a book called the Classic of Mountains and Seas that says it is 'shaped like a turtle, white body and red head', and 'can ward off fire'."

A pebble rolled down the cliff and landed on its shell; it didn't stir. A beetle crawled out of the fallen rock and passed right under its nose; it didn't stir. The beetle reached the pool and touched the water, and the head came out — snap. Every so often it put its own head down into the pool, reached the bottom, and drew back — there was a hand's depth left, and the rock round the pool was ringed with water marks, the highest level with the top of its shell. It was dying of thirst. The new crack at the rim of its shell seeped black. Xiaoman looked at the hollow again: oval, pointed at one end, a small dip at each of its four sides — the same size as that iron pot. He thought: what this wall wants is that weight.

He couldn't beat it. He had seen that flick of the sleeve on the riverbank; the one who flicked it had been one mouthful for this. His father used to say: "What you can't beat, you don't fight. You hang it a deadfall."

exits.means: tries to pry the gui off the wall by force — the shell does not budge, it bites, the wall stays shut

snub.zh: 你拿竹筒去撬那口铁锅，撬了三回，纹丝不动；第四回，它一口咬在你手背上，血珠子冒了出来。壳沿上一道一道的旧印子，刀砍的，铁器撬的——前人也这么撬过。墙，没开。
snub.en: You lever at the iron pot with your flask, three times; it doesn't budge. The fourth time it bites the back of your hand and beads of blood well up. Along the rim of its shell run old marks — knife cuts, the scrape of iron levers: those before you pried too. The wall stays shut.

exits.means: turns the gui over, then pours it his three days' water; it crawls into its hollow at the wall's foot — it is the latch — and the wall opens
exits._grant: 古四 (2026-10-02): the 饭桶 spat out 踏马的符 for one of 银月's tail hairs; he never tried it, folded it into his belt fold. An exit grants one item, and 古四's two (wm-danlu keep, wm-diyilu save) already carry the 饭桶 and the 回春丹 — so the bag gets it here, the first free step before the chase. One use: its card summons the 蛫 as a 护主 against 邹青松's 四蛇合围; he slaps it on blind (作者: 「这个用完就没了，留在秘境里用。」).

story.zh:
他等那颗脑袋缩稳了，才从石缝里溜下来，贴着崖根摸到塌石边，捡起那把剑。剑刃上一个缺口也没有。他爬上浅窝上头那块石檐，解下包袱的背绳，把剑尖朝下绑在一块斗大的石头底下；石头搁在檐口上，只搁了一半，背绳一头拴着石头，一头垂下来，拴在竹筒上。他溜下来，拔了竹筒塞子，把三天的水一口不剩，全倒进了那个浅窝，竹筒搁在窝底。银月道：「那是你三天的水。」小满道：「墙后头有风，风里有潮气。有潮气，就有水。」

水声一响，那颗脑袋出来了。它闻了一闻，四条腿撑起那口铁锅，一步一挪，挪进了浅窝。壳一落进去，严丝合缝，墙里头「轰隆隆」一阵闷响。它把脖子伸得老长，去够窝底那只竹筒——绳子一紧，檐上的石头翻了下来，剑尖朝下，正扎进壳沿靠脖子那道裂纹里。

它没有死。它是活了不知几百年的东西，挨了这一下，整口铁锅掀起半尺来高，那颗脑袋甩回来，一口咬住了伏在窝边的小满的左小臂，牙进了肉，咬到了骨头，一扯，把他拖倒在壳沿上。那张嘴不松，脑袋往壳里缩，要把他的胳膊一起拖进去。小满抽不出手，也没有运功。剑柄就在它脖子边上，离那张嘴不到一尺。他两只脚蹬住窝沿，右手攥住剑柄，拿整个身子的分量往下压。一寸，又一寸。那张嘴越咬越紧，又一点一点地松了。

那面墙从正中裂开了一道缝，一股风从缝里涌出来，扑在他脸上，暖得像春天。小满掰开那张嘴，把胳膊抽出来，撕下一截袄襟缠上，血一会儿就透了。他看着窝底那只翻倒的竹筒，一滴水也没剩，道：「那是三天的水。」顿了一顿，又道：「它在水里活了几百年。我却拿水骗了它。」银月半天才道：「它就是门闩。……这回，拔不出来了。」往年潭是满的，它不渴，一辈子没挪进那个窝；前人见了它，不是打，就是撬；这扇门，从来没开过。

便在这时，头顶上传来一阵脚步声，碎石子一阵一阵往下落。「——我就说他往这边走了！」
story.en:
He waited till the head was well in, then slid down out of the crack, edged along the foot of the cliff to the fallen rock, and picked up the sword. Not a nick on the blade. He climbed onto the stone eave above the hollow, untied the strap of his bundle and lashed the sword point-down under a rock the size of a grain measure; the rock he set on the lip of the eave, only half on, the strap tied round it at one end and the other end hanging down to his bamboo flask. He slid down again, pulled the flask's stopper, poured his three days' water, every last drop, into the hollow, and left the flask lying at the bottom. "That was your three days' water," said Yinyue. "There's wind behind the wall, and damp in the wind. Where there's damp there's water," said Xiaoman.

At the sound of water the head came out. It sniffed, then heaved the iron pot up on four legs and shuffled, one step at a time, into the hollow. The shell settled in without a gap, and a deep rumble ran through the wall. It stretched its neck out long to reach the flask at the bottom — the strap went taut, the rock on the eave tipped over, and the sword came down point-first, straight into the crack where the rim met the neck.

It didn't die. It had lived who knew how many hundred years; at the blow the whole iron pot heaved half a foot off the ground, and the head whipped round and caught Xiaoman's left forearm where he crouched at the hollow's edge, teeth through the flesh, down to the bone, and one wrench dragged him down across the rim of the shell. The jaws didn't let go; the head was pulling back into the shell, and his arm with it. Xiaoman couldn't pull free, and didn't use his cultivation. The hilt stood right beside its neck, less than a foot from those jaws. He braced both feet against the hollow's rim, gripped the hilt with his right hand and bore down with the whole weight of his body. An inch, then another. The jaws clamped tighter, and then, little by little, slackened.

The wall split down the middle and a wind poured through the crack into his face, warm as spring. Xiaoman pried the jaws apart, drew out his arm, tore a strip from his jacket and bound it; the blood soaked through in no time. He looked at the overturned flask at the bottom of the hollow, not a drop left in it, and said: "That was three days' water." A pause. "It's lived in water for hundreds of years. And I tricked it with water." It was a long while before Yinyue said: "It is the latch. …This time it won't come out." In other years the pool was full; it was never thirsty and never in its life shifted into that hollow. Those before him had met it and either struck or pried; this door had never opened.

Just then footsteps sounded overhead and pebbles came rattling down. "— I told you he went this way!"

withdrawn.zh: 蛫缩回了潭里，把赤红的头又探了出来，一眨不眨地盯着你。——再来。
withdrawn.en: The gui draws back into the pool, then pokes its red head out again and stares at you unblinking. — Again.
